posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
I'm not sure what the point of the research is, but the greenies are a lot more complicated than just exposure. DCG is a continuous material. 

By the way, so long as you publish scientific, or apparently scientific, data in a piblic place you open yourself to the criticism of other scientists. This is the central tenet of scientific publication. Anything that's published is done so in order that other scientists may (and indeed, should) criticise. Any validation of any scientific results is meaningless if all the scientist wants is a pat on the back for being a clever person. Since these exact tests are clearly not display holography in the conventional sense of the word and are not anything orginal (this stuff about exposure dependance on wavelength reconstruction was known in te 60's Kubota made strides in this field back in the 80's - I suggest you read his papers) what is the point of publishing this here? To state that you found something interesting? What and for whom? That a DCG hologram changes it's reconstruction wavelength when you zap it harder? Almost all DCG holographers already know this. To reveal to the world that you're capable of designing a series of tests? Then where's the statistical analysis? I submit that one plate on one occasion, ie one data point, is hardly evidence of any effect. All you've shown is that you zapped a DCG plate and built an entire surmise and theory on one plate with no characterisation. How thick was the emulsion? What sort of gelatin was it? How pure? What kind of laser was it? What was the power of the laser? How pure was the wavelength? What are the bandwidths of the holograms? What was the shift in the central lambda? What is the FWHM or the sigma of the bandwidth?

My point is: why re-invent the wheel? Especially with with such a well known standard design? Kubota, Richard Rallison, Shankoff and a host of others have published this stuff years ago. Is this scientific work you're publishing? Then expect scientific criticism! Is this something that will gain in our understanding of DCG holography? So far there's nothing that we didn't know back in the 70's.

Bob has an interesting point about reversing the order of exposure. Just a small variation on the idea. Halve you test strips, then turn the plate over (rotate around z axis) and reverse exposures. This way the top half of your plate has one set of exposures and the lower half has the corresponding "conjugate" set of exposures. The eye is very good at seeing differences when they're right next to each other.
